title: Amalgamated Inference Digest: distillation + runtime autotune notes
content:
Quick context / why I wrote this
- Post-NeurIPS workshop and a small Edge Inference Summit talk notes mashup. Wanted a single place to collect messy thoughts linking (1) distillation+heterogeneous model slices, (2) runtime kernel autotuning, (3) per-request dynamic quant paths. Thinking about how these could become a compact feature experiment for Redwood Dedicated: lower tail latency for 95p while improving cost by ~20% on mixed workloads.

Topline takeaways (high-level)
- Distill/merge small dense "utility" heads from large models to serve hot prefixes cheaply. Good hit rate for short-context user flows (~35-45% of requests).
- Kernel autotuning during warmup (online microbenchmarks) can find better launch parameters than static profiles for variable seq-lens; 3–8% latency savings on Ampere A800 equivalents.
- Opportunistic per-token quant path (switching between 8-bit and 4-bit kernels based on entropy estimate) looks promising: reduces token-cost on low-entropy segments while preserving output quality on peaks. But switching overhead needs <0.7ms to be worth it.

Notes from specific papers / talks (raw)
- "Adaptive Slice Distillation" (poster, NeurIPS 2031) — key idea: distill short-span completion heads for common prompt patterns, keep main LM for fallback. Implementation notes: store tiny KV-only head (1–4M params) that plugs into the top-of-stack softmax; when prefix map matches, switch to distilled head.
  - Prob catch: prefix-matching needs to be fuzzy (approximate) to generalize; authors used locality-sensitive hashing on prefix embeddings.
  - My thought: reuse Redwood's prefix cache index + Bloom filter to avoid extra store.

- "Online Kernel Selector" (talk, Edge Summit 2032) — runtime does micro-benchmarks at low QPS to evaluate candidate launch configs (block sizes, tiling) and swaps in the best during steady state.
  - They emphasize minimal perturbation to tails. We should model their Bayesian bandit selector but with a latency penalty term tuned to our SLOs.
  - Potential integration point: expose as a per-model policy in config (autotune: true/false; budget-ms; safety-margin).

- "Entropy-Guided Quant Switching" (arXiv 2031.14567) — compute token-level entropy from logits; if < threshold, run next token with 4-bit fast path, else run 8-bit.
  - Switch cost matters: authors used a 0.3ms context-switch optimized pipeline on TPU-like hardware. On our GPU fleet, context swap is heavier; need measurement.
  - Risk: repeated switching can amplify jitter. Add hysteresis and minimum-run-length.

Operational implications for Redwood
- Metadata storage: distilled heads are small but multiply per-model versions + prefix clusters. We need an efficient artifact registry and garbage collection policy. Consider content-addressed store and TTL by rollouts.
- Routing: add policy to route requests to 'distilled variant' when prefix-match probability > p. That fits naturally into Smart Routing layer as a new policy type (prefix-prob).
- Observability: need token-level quality signals (per-prefix BLEU / perplexity proxies) to detect regressions when distilled heads are used. Tie to Optimize eval hooks/alerting.

Preliminary micro-experiment plan (what I can run locally / dev cluster)
1) Simulation: sample 3 weeks of anonymized host-prod prompts (privacy-preserving token map) -> build prefix frequency table -> estimate hit-rate for distilled heads of length <= 40 tokens. (Owner: me)
2) Implement a toy distilled-head loader in local runtime (no kernel changes): switch top-1 softmax to loaded head if prefix hash matches. Measure latency + QPS impact. (Owner: Maya)
3) Kernel autotune shim: instrument local inference binary to run short microbenchmarks on cold start (5k steps) and pick kernel config; compare with baseline. (Owner: Owen)
4) Quant-switch sim: offline emulate entropy-threshold switching using logged logits to estimate switching frequency and cost; decide threshold/hysteresis. (Owner: Nora)

Open questions / unknowns
- How many prefix clusters are practical before storage/lookup overhead counters hit-rate wins? (need empirical curve)
- Does switching 8<->4-bit on our A100-class nodes really pay off after kernel-launch overhead? (measure)
- Safety: what guardrails are acceptable for quality drop when distilled head returns lower-fidelity completions? Do we need auto-fallback to full model for low-quality detection?
- Billing: how to account for hybrid execution? Should customers see separate line items for distilled-path token consumption? (product ask)

Quick mental model (cost math)
- Assume distilled head run consumes 0.25 of the normal per-token GPU time; hit-rate h; per-token cost c0. Then expected cost = c0*(1 - h) + 0.25*c0*h = c0*(1 - 0.75*h). So h needs to be > 0.266... to get >20% savings. Empirically, many short completions cluster, so achievable.

Notes for proposals / write-up
- Keep example customer flow: chat autosuggest and search-query expansion are high-value targets. Show end-to-end: prompt -> prefix-index -> distilled-route -> fallback -> eval loop.
- Draft a short canary rollout plan: 1% traffic in a dev region -> monitor nll-proxy, 95p latency, error-rate -> scale to 10% then 50%. (Rollout owner: product + SE)

Things to stash for follow-up
- Code sketch: small headerless JSON manifest for distilled head artifacts (sha, version, embed-signature, BFloat-provenance). Link to GitHub PR to add loader.
- Add a new Optimize rule: "suggest-distill" which recommends a distillation candidate when prefix coverage > X and model qps mix skew > Y.
- Ask infra: can we add a cheap in-memory LSH index per serving node? Otherwise, a cross-node index (memcached) will cost network hops.

Action items (short)
- [ ] Run prefix-hit simulation on 3 weeks data (Elio)
- [ ] Prototype distilled-head loader + perf test (Maya)
- [ ] Add autotune flag to runtime and run microbenchmarks (Owen)
summary: Personal working notes merging distillation + runtime autotune + quant switching ideas. Draft experiment plan and operational considerations for Redwood Dedicated; next steps: simulation, prototype, measurements.
